title: Resource Development: Acquire Infrastructure (Botnet) + Collection: Screen Capture
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II

mitre_stages.note: Attacker builds or rents a botnet of compromised hosts as attack infrastructure.
Bot-infected host captures screenshots for exfiltration back to the operator.

description: This dataset attack label spans a botnet's two functional roles: acquiring/operating the botnet infrastructure itself, and the infected host performing screen-capture data collection on behalf of the operator. Periodic beaconing over HTTP/HTTPS is a common transport pattern for both stages, but transport-layer camouflage is not itself the technique captured here.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Regular 'heartbeat' signals (beacons) from the infected host to an external controller, often masked as legitimate web browsing.

mitigation.name: Network Intrusion Prevention
mitigation.action: Identify and block known C2 IP addresses and domains using reputation-based filtering.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Implement strict outbound traffic filtering and deep packet inspection to identify non-standard protocol usage over web ports.

false_positive_hints: Background update services, telemetry, and legitimate cloud-sync applications often use periodic HTTP communication.

title: Brute Force: Password Guessing (Web Application Login)
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II
description: Adversaries may attempt to gain access to a web application by systematically trying many username/password combinations against its login form, without knowledge of valid credentials.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Repeated HTTP POST requests to a login endpoint with varying credential payloads, from a single or small set of source IPs.

mitigation.name: Account Use Policies
mitigation.action: Implement account lockout or rate-limiting after repeated failed login attempts.

mitigation.name: Multi-factor Authentication
mitigation.action: Require MFA on web application login to reduce the impact of guessed credentials.

false_positive_hints: Load-testing tools or misconfigured client applications retrying failed logins can resemble brute force traffic.

title: Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood (HOIC)
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II
description: Adversaries may cause a DoS by exhausting the resources of an endpoint's application layer. HOIC (High Orbit Ion Cannon) coordinates many hosts to send high-volume HTTP requests, often with randomized headers via 'boosters', to exhaust server resources and evade simple filtering.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Coordinated high-volume HTTP requests from multiple source IPs, with randomized headers to defeat basic signature and caching defenses.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Rate-limit and geo-filter traffic at the edge; deploy a CDN/WAF with DDoS scrubbing.

mitigation.name: Exploit Protection
mitigation.action: Use behavioral anomaly detection to identify coordinated multi-source request floods.

false_positive_hints: Legitimate flash-crowd traffic (e.g. viral content, product launches) can produce similar high-volume, multi-source HTTP patterns.

title: Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood (LOIC HTTP)
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II
description: Adversaries may cause a DoS by exhausting the resources of an endpoint's application layer. LOIC (Low Orbit Ion Cannon) in HTTP mode floods a target with HTTP GET/POST requests from multiple coordinated hosts to exhaust web server threads and connections.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Rapid, repeated HTTP GET/POST requests from multiple coordinated source IPs with minimal inter-arrival time between requests.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Rate-limit per-IP request rate and deploy a CDN/WAF with DDoS scrubbing.

mitigation.name: Exploit Protection
mitigation.action: Use connection/thread limits and behavioral anomaly detection to identify coordinated request floods.

false_positive_hints: Aggressive web crawlers or misconfigured monitoring tools polling frequently can resemble low-and-fast HTTP flood traffic.

title: Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood (LOIC UDP)
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II
description: A UDP flood is a type of denial-of-service attack in which a large number of User Datagram Protocol (UDP) packets are sent to a targeted server with the aim of overwhelming that device's ability to process and respond.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Flood of UDP packets often with spoofed source IPs targeting random or specific ports.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Implement rate limiting for UDP traffic and block traffic to unused ports.

mitigation.name: Exploit Protection
mitigation.action: Use DDoS mitigation services that can distinguish between legitimate UDP traffic and a flood.

false_positive_hints: High-volume media streaming or online gaming can generate significant UDP traffic.

title: DoS GoldenEye Attack
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II
description: GoldenEye is a DoS tool that performs a layer 7 DoS attack by exhausting the application pool resources. It uses Keep-Alive and Cache-Control headers to persist connections.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Persistent HTTP connections with high request rates designed to exhaust server-side resources.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Implement rate limiting and connection limits per source IP.

mitigation.name: Exploit Protection
mitigation.action: Use WAF to detect and block GoldenEye-specific request patterns.

false_positive_hints: Aggressive web crawlers or misconfigured client applications might generate similar high-frequency request patterns.

title: Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood (HULK)
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II
description: Adversaries may attempt to cause a denial of service (DoS) by sending a high volume of network traffic directly to a target. This specific profile mimics the HULK (Http Unbearable Load King) tool, which generates unique HTTP requests to exhaust server resources and bypass caching.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Massive volume of unique HTTP GET requests with randomized headers (User-Agent, Referer) to prevent server-side caching and exhaust the application pool.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Use upstream filtering services (ISP/CDN) to intercept traffic before it reaches the target network.

mitigation.name: Network Intrusion Prevention
mitigation.action: Implement signature-based or anomaly-based IDS/IPS to detect and block HULK-specific request patterns.

false_positive_hints: Legitimate flash crowds or aggressive web crawlers can sometimes generate high volumes of unique requests.

title: Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood (Slowhttptest)
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II
description: Slowhttptest is a highly configurable tool that simulates some Application Layer Denial of Service attacks. It implements most common low-bandwidth Application Layer DoS attacks.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Slowly sending HTTP headers or POST bodies to keep connections open as long as possible.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Limit connection duration and request header/body timeout.

mitigation.name: Exploit Protection
mitigation.action: Implement minimum data rate requirements for incoming connections.

false_positive_hints: Mobile users on poor signal or proxies with high latency can occasionally mimic slow HTTP behaviors.

title: Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion (Slowloris)
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II
description: Adversaries may cause a DoS by exhausting resources on an endpoint service. Slowloris achieves this by opening many connections and keeping them open as long as possible by sending partial HTTP requests.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Persistent connections with minimal data throughput, holding server threads open indefinitely to prevent legitimate users from connecting.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Implement connection limits per IP and reduce timeouts for incomplete HTTP requests.

mitigation.name: Exploit Protection
mitigation.action: Use reverse proxies or load balancers that buffer entire requests before passing them to the backend.

false_positive_hints: Clients on extremely slow or congested networks may exhibit behaviors similar to low-and-slow attacks.

title: Brute Force: Password Guessing (FTP)
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II
description: Adversaries may use brute force techniques to attempt access to valid accounts by guessing passwords. This profile focuses on FTP services where numerous login attempts are made systematically.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Frequent, rapid connection attempts to port 21, typically with small packet sizes representing repetitive USER and PASS commands.

mitigation.name: Account Use Policies
mitigation.action: Implement account lockout policies after a threshold of failed login attempts.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Limit the rate of connection attempts from a single source IP to the FTP service.

false_positive_hints: Misconfigured automated backup scripts or users with expired credentials can cause bursts of failed login attempts.

title: Execution: User Execution (Malicious File) + Discovery: Network Service Scanning
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II

mitre_stages.note: Victim opens a malicious file to establish the initial foothold.
Attacker scans the internal network from the compromised host to map reachable services.

description: This dataset attack label spans two stages: a malicious file is opened to gain an initial foothold on the host, followed by internal network service scanning from the compromised machine. This can include buffer overflows, path traversal, or remote code execution as the initial vector.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Initial exploit payload followed by persistent command and control traffic or data exfiltration.

mitigation.name: Update Software
mitigation.action: Regularly patch and update all software and operating systems.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Use network segmentation to limit the impact of a successful infiltration.

false_positive_hints: Unusual but legitimate administrative activity or specialized software updates can sometimes mimic infiltration patterns.

title: SSH Brute Force Attack
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II
description: Adversaries may attempt to gain access to an SSH server by systematically trying many passwords or passphrases.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Rapid sequence of connection attempts to port 22 with characteristic packet sizes for SSH authentication.

mitigation.name: Account Use Policies
mitigation.action: Implement fail2ban or similar tools to block IPs after multiple failed SSH logins.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Disable password authentication and use SSH keys instead.

false_positive_hints: Automated administration scripts with expired credentials can trigger multiple failed login attempts.

title: Anomaly: Potential Novel Attack or Zero-day (Unclassified)
description: This profile represents a network behavior that deviates significantly from the normal baseline but does not match any known attack signatures or MITRE ATT&CK techniques in the current database. This could indicate a zero-day exploit, a novel evasion technique, or a misconfigured internal service.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: Observed behavior is statistically improbable based on training data. Characteristics may include unusual packet size distributions, unconventional flag combinations, or unprecedented traffic volume for the target service.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Isolate the involved hosts and perform manual forensic analysis to determine the nature of the anomaly.

mitigation.name: Network Intrusion Prevention
mitigation.action: Implement strict egress filtering to prevent potential data exfiltration from the suspicious host.

false_positive_hints: New software deployments, unexpected system updates, or hardware failures can cause deviations that appear as anomalies.

title: Initial Access: Exploit Public-Facing Application (SQL Injection)
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II
description: Adversaries may attempt to exploit vulnerabilities in internet-facing applications to gain access. SQL injection targets flaws in the database query logic of web applications.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: HTTP GET/POST requests containing encoded SQL syntax, unusual escape characters, or boolean logic probes.

mitigation.name: Exploit Protection
mitigation.action: Enforce input validation and use parameterized queries in application code.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Deploy WAF rules to identify and block common SQL injection signatures.

false_positive_hints: Search queries or form submissions containing apostrophes or technical language can occasionally trigger SQLi alerts.

title: Initial Access: Drive-by Compromise (Cross-Site Scripting)
mitre_source: Borisenko et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1109/SYNCHROINFO55067.2022.9840920, Table II
description: Adversaries may attempt to exploit vulnerabilities in internet-facing applications to gain access. Cross-site scripting (XSS) injects malicious client-side scripts into a web application's input fields to be executed in a victim's browser.

network_indicators.traffic_pattern: HTTP requests containing script-like payloads (e.g. angle brackets, encoded JavaScript) submitted through form fields or URL parameters.

mitigation.name: Exploit Protection
mitigation.action: Enforce output encoding and input sanitization on all user-controllable fields.

mitigation.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigation.action: Deploy WAF rules to identify and block common XSS payload signatures.

false_positive_hints: Legitimate content containing HTML-like text or code snippets (e.g. developer forums) can occasionally trigger XSS pattern alerts.
